nameStory: This delicate hydroid was named after the Carolinas, where it was first scientifically described. The genus Bougainvillia honors French explorer Louis Antoine de Bougainville, who sailed around the world in the 1760s and whose name also graces the colorful tropical vine bougainvillea.
description: The Carolina hydroid is a tiny colonial marine animal that looks like a miniature underwater tree or fern. It grows as branching colonies up to 2-3 inches tall, with a brownish stem and delicate, transparent feeding polyps that extend from the branches like tiny flowers. Each colony is made up of hundreds of individual animals called polyps that work together, filter-feeding on microscopic plankton and organic particles in the water.

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Forms irregular, bushy colonies with multiple branching stems that feel slightly rough and wiry to the touch when out of water

idTips.label: Feeding polyps
idTips.description: Tiny transparent bell-shaped polyps extend from branch tips, each with 4-6 delicate tentacles that wave gently in the current

idTips.label: Colony size
idTips.description: Reaches 1-3 inches in height, feeling quite delicate and easily broken when handled

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows attached to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings by a tangled mass of root-like structures

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Main stem appears brownish or amber-colored, while the living polyps are nearly transparent with a slight pinkish tinge

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's coast, typically growing on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, pier pilings, and boat hulls in harbors and protected bays. Prefers areas with gentle water movement where it can filter-feed effectively, usually in depths of 3-30 feet.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin active growth as water temperatures rise, with new polyps budding from existing branches.
seasonality.summer: Peak growth period when colonies are most visible and robust, actively feeding and reproducing.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may begin to decline as temperatures drop, though some may persist in warmer protected waters.
seasonality.winter: Most colonies die back in colder New England waters, surviving as dormant stages or in deeper, more stable temperature zones.

funFact: This tiny animal is actually more closely related to jellyfish than to plants, and its colonies can produce free-swimming baby jellyfish no bigger than a pinhead that eventually settle down to start new colonies elsewhere!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small seaweeds or other hydroids, but unlike algae, it has distinct animal-like polyps with tentacles that move independently. Other branching hydroids can look similar, but the specific branching pattern and polyp arrangement help distinguish species.
contextualKnowledge: Many people mistake hydroids for seaweeds or small corals, but they're actually cnidarians - the same group that includes jellyfish and sea anemones. The colonial lifestyle where many individual animals work together as one organism is a fascinating evolutionary strategy.
compareHints: Since this is the only Bougainvillia species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small branching hydroids in the family. Carolina hydroids tend to have more irregular branching compared to the more symmetrical patterns of related species, and their polyps are arranged differently along the branches than most other local hydroids.
